Token
TOH-ken
n.
Old English tacen, a sign. Webster 1828: a sign; something intended to represent or indicate another thing or an event. In the Authorized Version the word is covenantal before it is anything else: the rainbow, circumcision, and the passover blood are all called tokens of a covenant.

Biblical Definition

A token in Scripture is a visible sign attached by God to a promise. After the flood He says three times over that the bow is one: This is the token of the covenant which I make between me and you and every living creature (Genesis 9:12); I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth (Genesis 9:13); This is the token of the covenant, which I have established between me and all flesh (Genesis 9:17). Circumcision is the same: ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you (Genesis 17:11). The exodus deliverance is bound on the hand and the forehead for a token upon thine hand, and for frontlets between thine eyes (Exodus 13:16). Rahab asks the spies for a true token that her house will be spared (Joshua 2:12), and receives the scarlet line. David prays, Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it (Psalm 86:17). The New Testament keeps the word for a sign that reads two ways at once: the courage of a persecuted church is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God (Philippians 1:28). And the darkest use is Judas’s kiss, a token agreed in advance (Mark 14:44).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TOKEN as a sign; something intended to represent or indicate another thing or an event; a mark; and, in a second sense, a memorial of friendship, an evidence of affection.

expand to see more

TOKEN, n. — A sign; something intended to represent or indicate another thing or an event; as, the rainbow is a token of God’s covenant.

A mark; as, the tokens of a disease.

A memorial of friendship; something by which the friendship of another person is to be kept in mind.

Webster’s first illustration is Genesis 9 itself. The token is not the covenant; it is the sign appointed to it, and its whole force comes from the word of the God who appointed it.

Key Scripture

Genesis 9:13 — "I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth."

Genesis 17:11 — "And ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you."

Exodus 13:16 — "And it shall be for a token upon thine hand, and for frontlets between thine eyes: for by strength of hand the LORD brought us forth out of Egypt."

Psalm 86:17 — "Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it, and be ashamed: because thou, LORD, hast holpen me, and comforted me."

Philippians 1:28 — "And in nothing terrified by your adversaries: which is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God."

Modern Corruption

The token is corrupted when the sign is severed from the word that appointed it — a rainbow made into a symbol of something God never attached to it, and covenant signs treated as either empty pictures or as conveying grace by the act itself.

expand to see more

Genesis 9 says three times what the bow means, and it means what God said. It is the token of a covenant that He will not again destroy the earth by a flood, and He states that the bow is set there so that I will look upon it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant. The sign points at God’s memory, not at ours, and it belongs to His promise and not to any human cause. To take the same arc and attach a different meaning to it — to make it the emblem of a movement whose defining claim is that Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 do not bind — is to take a covenant sign and hang another covenant on it. The dictionary states this plainly rather than obliquely: the bow is God’s, and its meaning was fixed before any of us arrived.

The second corruption is sacramental and runs in two directions. Circumcision was a token of the covenant, and Paul says of Abraham that he received it as a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised (Romans 4:11) — sign and seal of a righteousness already possessed by faith, not the means of obtaining it. Rome’s error is to make the sign convey grace by the working of the work; bare memorialism’s error is to make it a picture with nothing in it. The Reformed position holds both: baptism and the Lord’s Supper are signs and seals in which Christ is truly present to the believer by faith, and empty to the one who comes without it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew is 'oth, a sign, the same word used of the signs in Egypt and of the sabbath; the Greek endeixis in Philippians 1:28 means a demonstration or proof shown forth.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'oth (H226) — a sign, token, mark; the rainbow (Genesis 9:12-17), circumcision (Genesis 17:11), the sabbath (Exodus 31:13).

Hebrew 'oth emeth — a true token; what Rahab asks of the spies (Joshua 2:12), answered by the scarlet line.

Hebrew mopheth (H4159) — a wonder or sign; often paired with 'oth in the exodus narratives.

Greek endeixis (G1732) — a showing forth, demonstration, proof; an evident token of perdition (Philippians 1:28).

Greek semeion (G4592) — a sign; the standard New Testament word, and the term John uses for the miracles of Christ.

Usage

"It shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth (Genesis 9:13) — the meaning of the bow is fixed by the God who set it."

"A token of the covenant betwixt me and you (Genesis 17:11) — circumcision as sign and seal, not as the means of righteousness."

"An evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation (Philippians 1:28) — one sign read two ways, and God is the one who gives it."
